summary: An April 1st humor RFC suggesting new MIME types such as electronic staples and paper clips for tying documents together. It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke imagines electronic staples and paper clips that hold digital documents together. It describes increasingly elaborate features in a serious tone.

subtitle: An April 1st parody that imagines electronic staples and paper clips for documents.

tldr.problem: This RFC does not solve a technical problem; it jokes about associating digital documents with office supplies.
tldr.mechanism: It imagines staple and paper-clip media types, complete with appearance settings, recycling, patents, and safety warnings.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st joke is informational and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1927 is an Informational April 1st joke about fictional electronic staples and paper clips.

sections.title: A Joke About Binding Digital Documents
sections.content:
This April 1st memo suggests new MIME types called “staple” and “paper clip” for associating parts of multipart documents. It contrasts documents that should stay together with ones meant to be spread apart.

The proposal is presented as a series of suggestions, not as a formal registration. The RFC says it does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo jokes that digital documents need electronic office supplies. Staples would keep items together, while clips would allow them to be separated.

sections.title: Imagined Features and Custom Appearance
sections.content:
The memo suggests hierarchical sizes, visible icons, and “color=” and “shape=” attributes for customizing clips. A “src=” attribute could point to an image, and the document even mentions three-dimensional models for virtual-reality headsets.

It also imagines certificates attached to each staple or clip to support accounting and detect unauthorized copying. These ideas parody the complexity of technical proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: The imagined clips could have colors, shapes, and pictures. The RFC extends the joke to patents, certificates, and 3D models.

sections.title: Recycling, Page Flags, and Warnings
sections.content:
The memo proposes looking for reusable clips when a file or folder is deleted, and bending clips into desktop sculptures. It also suggests attaching a clip to one page or a particular passage in a larger document.

Its final warnings claim electronic clips could be unsafe around small children or damage floppy disks. The security section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke imagines recycling clips and using them to mark pages. It ends with absurd warnings about digital clips and floppy disks.
